Regarding CPU driver overhead: as mentioned in this video, I recommend watching reviews that had time to test lower end CPUs as well. Gamers Nexus saw almost no difference on a 12400 and ryzen 5600, while noting that they conjecture that more differences would show in games reaching extremely high FPS: https://youtu.be/m9uK4D35FlM?si=QlLhL2soDEyAwyAh. Hardware Unboxed also tested on an Ryzen 5600: https://youtu.be/buJSNbVYxVA?si=-RMyjlQ2Ly29WrXM and noticed several cases where that did reduce the performance of the B570, but it is important to note that overall it was just a several percentage point reduction to the average. My conclusion is that I stand by what I said at the end of this video which is that it is certainly something worth noting, especially on an extremely low end and/or old CPU, but that these issues mostly show up when reaching high framerates, which is often not what cards in this class are typically able to achieve. I am sure that some specific games may be more problematic than typical (but this tends to be the case with Arc in general- it is still generally less consistent in performance when compared to AMD and Nvidia across a wide variety of games). The most important issue (again as noted in this video) is making sure that your motherboard/CPU platform supports resize BAR. If it does not, then you should not consider Arc GPUs.

text:
No, because the people who buy graphics cards at this price point don't have new cutting-edge CPU's, and the Intel cards fall off a cliff when going even just back to a popular mid-range Zen 3 processor.

Unless/until Intel can solve this problem, Battlemage cards will remain a strange niche, assuming you can even buy them.  Demand the B570 seems considerably lower than for the B580 so far, but the latter hasn't been in stock for a month.  The B570 could very well be another paper launch but without the glowing reviews to sell out the meager initial stock.

Basically, all of your results here are invalid, because zero people will have a system with a 9800X3D and a B570.  Or B580, for that matter.  Literally zero.

While I'm dissatisfied with most of the content about the problems with Battlemage on slower CPU's because none of them have any metrics whatsoever about total system CPU usage or per-thread game CPU usage, there's no question that there's some kind of problem on these somewhat older and slower CPU's.  You don't have to go back more than two generations to see it, either.  In some games, you can see it just by skipping X3D and staying with a modern Zen 5 processor (or, probably, an Intel one based on Raptor Lake - which shouldn't be used due to stability problems that nobody has confirmed to be fixed - or Arrow Lake - which is probably due a re-review to see where things actually stand now).

Assuming the issue is just more CPU overhead, then Intel is the worst, nVidia is second, and AMD the best (i.e. will lose the least going to slower and slower CPU's).  There are complicating factors with DX11 games, where nVidia drivers still have more overhead, but use some of that overhead to hijack draw calls from games and thread them, making the games themselves run faster provided there's sufficient CPU headroom to do so.

Overall, the kind of testing you're doing here, and which pretty much everyone else also does, is utterly insufficient to collect all the relevant information.  It's just the nature of the beast.  To do proper testing requires a team of people using multiple pieces of hardware, with sufficient overlap to account for any differences between the individual units.  Nobody does this.  The one organization which actually has to resources to do so, LMG, does an even worse job of comprehensive testing.
